title: Learning From Famous Decision-Makers
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article makes the case for reading leadership biographies as a substitute for the decision-making mentorship most people never get to witness firsthand. It argues that biographies reveal the hidden reasoning, competing pressures, and value trade-offs behind big calls in a way that day-to-day work rarely exposes. The author cautions against hero-worship, urging readers instead to extract specific transferable lessons rather than wholesale models to imitate. A short reading list is offered, spanning Steve Jobs, Phil Knight, Ruth Bader Ginsburg, the Wright brothers, and Indra Nooyi. The piece ends by inviting readers to reflect on what's currently on their own nightstand.
points: Biographies function as a stand-in for the real-time decision-making mentorship most leaders never get to observe.
Good biographies expose the hidden assumptions, values, and competing interests behind consequential decisions.
Readers should avoid over-extrapolating from any one leader's context and instead extract specific, transferable lessons.
A handful of recommended titles are offered as starting points, from Steve Jobs to Indra Nooyi's memoir.
quotes: By reading about how famous leaders faced difficult decisions, they get to learn how critical decisions unfold and get made behind the scenes.
Some of the best leaders are deliberate readers and their genre of choice is the biographies of famous decision-makers.
The best leaders and learners don’t over-extrapolate from a decision made by a famous leader from another time or context.
There is no optimal or flawless leader. But there are behaviors, routines, and practices that are universal and timeless in their application.
By grabbing a singular lesson from each biography, leaders soon develop their own unique decision-making style that propels them forward.
